chapter.name: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
chapter.blurb: The concluding chapter of the Grade 9 Exploration textbook, bringing the whole year's science together to view the Earth as one connected system of five spheres. Covers uneven heating of the Earth by solar radiation (the electromagnetic spectrum, insolation and the solar constant), why heating is uneven (albedo and latitude), the layered atmosphere and the greenhouse effect, the winds and ocean currents that uneven heating drives, the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen biogeochemical cycles, and how human activity disrupts -- and can help restore -- these processes.

scope_in.item: The Earth system is made up of five interacting spheres: geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere and biosphere
Geosphere examples: solid rocks, soil, landforms (Deccan plateau, Thar desert) and the Earth's interior
Hydrosphere examples: oceans, rivers (Ganga-Brahmaputra), lakes and groundwater
Cryosphere examples: Himalayan glaciers, snow in Ladakh and polar ice caps
Atmosphere: the air surrounding the Earth that we breathe
Biosphere examples: mangroves, forests, farms, ocean plankton and coral reefs

A disturbance in one sphere leads to changes in others (Activity 13.1: less snowfall -> lower lake level -> less grass; warmer Arabian Sea -> more evaporation -> monsoon variability -> floods/drought; melting glaciers -> flooding/rising sea level -> threatened coastal cities -> habitat loss)
Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at the speed of light and, unlike sound (a mechanical wave), need no medium
The electromagnetic spectrum runs from high frequency/short wavelength (gamma rays, X-rays -- high energy, harmful) to low frequency/long wavelength (infrared, radio waves)

About 99% of solar radiation reaching Earth is concentrated in the UV, visible and infrared range; gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered by the upper atmosphere; microwaves and radio waves carry very little energy

UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer; visible light powers photosynthesis and partly warms land/water; infrared warms the Earth's surface, which re-radiates heat, some of it trapped by greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour)

UV wavelength range 100-400 nm, higher energy than visible light; prolonged exposure risks to eyes/skin and cancer; protective measures (UV glasses, sunscreen); uses (killing germs in water purifiers, powering fluorescent lights)

Insolation = the amount of the Sun's radiation reaching the Earth's surface; the solar constant (about 1.4 kWm-2, or 1400 J s-1m-2) is the average solar energy reaching the top of the atmosphere before any absorption, scattering or reflection
Surface insolation is lower than the solar constant (about 1 kWm-2 under clear sky) because gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter some of the radiation first
India's tropical and sub-tropical location gives it abundant sunlight, driving the southwest monsoon and offering solar energy potential
Anna Mani and S. Rangarajan mapped solar insolation across India in the 1950s and published India's first insolation atlas, 'Solar Radiation Over India' (1982)
Calculating solar energy received using E = intensity x area x time (Example 13.1)

Albedo = the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface; high-albedo surfaces (snow, ice) stay cool, low-albedo surfaces (black soil, ocean water) heat faster; dark surfaces absorb more, light surfaces reflect more
Named albedo values from Table 13.1: snow 0.80-0.90, ice 0.50-0.70, crushed rock 0.25-0.30

The urban heat island effect: cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas because built materials (steel, concrete, brick, asphalt) absorb, retain and re-radiate heat, increasing energy demand for cooling; rural/forest areas stay cooler through shade and plant transpiration

Latitude and Earth's shape: because Earth is spherical, the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles, concentrating radiation over a smaller area at the equator and spreading it over a larger area near the poles, causing equator-pole temperature differences
Earth's spherical shape and axial tilt cause seasons and changing daytime length (recap)
The atmosphere is held in place by Earth's gravity and consists mainly of nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases

The layered structure of the atmosphere: troposphere (0-12 km, nearly all weather, temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 degC/km, tallest above the equator, lowest above the poles); stratosphere (12-50 km, contains the ozone layer, temperature increases with height, calming the layer and confining weather to the troposphere); mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere named as playing only a minor role in surface climate; outer space begins at about 100 km

The atmosphere's two crucial roles: partly absorbing incoming solar radiation (ozone blocks UV, clouds/gases absorb some sunlight) and trapping outgoing heat via greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour), keeping the Earth warm enough for life
Excess CO2 from human activity enhances the greenhouse effect, causing global warming
Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun, because Venus's atmosphere causes an uncontrolled greenhouse effect
K.R. Ramanathan measured ozone levels in the Himalayas (1934, 18,000 feet), found them lower than expected, and later led early monsoon forecasting efforts

The ozone layer as a protective shield against UV; CFCs (used in refrigerators and aerosols) caused the Antarctic ozone hole; the Montreal Protocol reduced CFC use and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering
Wind is the movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure, mainly caused by uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun

Local winds: valley breeze (daytime, warm air rising off sun-facing slopes, cooler valley air replacing it) and mountain breeze (night-time, slopes cooling faster, air flowing down into the valley); examples given: Shimla, Dehradun, other Himalayan valleys

Planetary winds: pressure belts (equatorial low, sub-tropical high around 30 degN/S, sub-polar low around 60 degN/S, polar high around 90 degN/S) formed by uneven heating between equator and poles, with Earth's rotation deflecting winds into curved paths (right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern Hemisphere)

Ocean currents: the continuous movement of large masses of ocean water, driven by planetary winds (surface friction), differences in temperature and salinity, Earth's rotation, and the distribution of land masses

Warm equatorial surface water travels toward the poles while colder, denser water returns at depth; lower-salinity water stays nearer the surface while higher-salinity, denser water sinks and moves at deeper levels

Earth's rotation deflects ocean currents into large circular gyres, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; continents further block and redirect currents

Ocean currents regulate climate by transporting heat from the equator towards the poles and support ecosystems by transporting nutrients; example: the North Atlantic Drift (an extension of the Gulf Stream) keeps north-western European ports ice-free in winter
IITM Pune runs computer models coupling energy flows between the atmosphere, oceans, land and ice to simulate and forecast the Indian monsoon
A biogeochemical cycle is the cyclic movement of matter and energy between abiotic and biotic components, recycling nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen

The water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, groundwater and runoff; how climate change intensifies rainfall/drought, raises sea levels and reduces groundwater recharge, linking the cryosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and biosphere

The carbon cycle: carbon circulates between the atmosphere (CO2), biosphere (plants/animals), geosphere (carbonate rocks, fossil fuels) and hydrosphere (dissolved CO2, marine shells); the fast cycle (photosynthesis/respiration/decomposition, days to years) and the slow cycle (fossil fuel formation and burning, millions of years)

The Keeling curve shows atmospheric CO2 rising about 35% from 1960 to 2025 (about 315 to 420 ppm), mainly due to fossil fuels and deforestation, with a seasonal sawtooth pattern caused by Northern Hemisphere plant growth
Carbon quantities named in the chapter: carbon is about 49% of the dry weight of living organisms; oceans hold about 71% of global carbon; the atmosphere holds only about 1%

The nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter converting N2 to ammonia), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter converting ammonia to nitrite to nitrate), assimilation by plants, ammonification by decomposers, and denitrification (Pseudomonas converting nitrate back to N2); lightning also fixes a small amount of nitrogen
The Haber-Bosch process artificially fixes nitrogen into ammonia for fertilisers, enabling India's Green Revolution, though it is energy intensive and fertiliser overuse degrades soil and water
The oxygen cycle: about 21% of the atmosphere is free O2; respiration and combustion consume O2 and release CO2; photosynthesis restores O2 using sunlight, water and CO2
Human impact: excess CO2 makes oceans more acidic, threatening plankton and coral reefs, while warmer oceans absorb CO2 less effectively as a carbon sink
Overuse of fertilisers causes eutrophication (excess nitrate leading to algal blooms, depleted oxygen and fish deaths), threatening water bodies and coastal fisheries
Deforestation effects: decreased photosynthesis and transpiration lowering local rainfall, altered albedo, increased soil erosion, and habitat loss leading to biodiversity decline
Vehicular emissions reacting with sunlight form ground-level smog and harmful ground-level ozone, distinct from the protective stratospheric ozone layer
Global cooperation can restore balance: the Montreal Protocol succeeded for the ozone layer, while the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement on CO2 emissions have been less successful

Restoration actions named in the chapter: renewable energy (solar, wind), planting trees, saving water, sustainable farming, and individual actions (reducing waste, reuse, recycling); India's Mission LiFE initiative

concepts.name: Earth as an Interconnected System of Spheres
concepts.description: Identifying Earth's five interacting spheres -- geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere and biosphere -- and explaining how a disturbance in one produces changes in the others.
concepts.idea: Earth is not five separate parts but one connected system; a change in one sphere ripples through the rest.
concepts.rule: The five spheres are geosphere (solid rock, soil, landforms, Earth's interior), hydrosphere (liquid surface water -- oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater), cryosphere (solid water -- ice and snow), atmosphere (the air surrounding Earth) and biosphere (all living organisms and their habitats); natural processes such as solar heating, air and water movement, and nutrient cycling connect them in a delicate balance, so a disturbance in one sphere changes the others.
concepts.example: Less snowfall in winter (cryosphere) means less water reaching a lake (hydrosphere) in summer, leaving less grass for sheep to graze (biosphere).

concepts.name: Solar Radiation, the EM Spectrum and Insolation
concepts.description: How electromagnetic radiation from the Sun reaches the Earth, what the electromagnetic spectrum contains, and how insolation and the solar constant describe how much of that energy actually reaches the surface.
concepts.idea: The Sun's electromagnetic radiation does not all reach or warm the Earth equally -- different parts of the spectrum behave differently, and only a fraction of the Sun's total output (the solar constant) actually reaches the surface as usable insolation.
concepts.rule: Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at the speed of light and, unlike sound, need no medium; the spectrum runs from high-energy, short-wavelength gamma rays and X-rays to low-energy, long-wavelength radio waves, with about 99% of the Sun's energy reaching Earth arriving as UV, visible and infrared radiation; the solar constant (about 1.4 kWm-2) is the energy reaching the top of the atmosphere, while insolation at the surface (about 1 kWm-2 under clear sky) is lower because gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter some of it on the way down.
concepts.example: In Example 13.1, at an insolation of 1 kWm-2, a 1 m2 area receives E = 1000 J s-1m-2 x 1 m2 x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J of energy in one hour -- about one unit of household electricity.

questions.a: The solar constant measures the energy reaching the top of the atmosphere before any absorption, scattering or reflection (about 1.4 kWm-2); surface insolation measures the energy actually reaching the ground after atmospheric absorption and scattering, so it is lower (about 1 kWm-2 under clear sky).

questions.a: Only a small fraction of the Sun's energy that reaches Earth is gamma rays and X-rays, since about 99% is concentrated in UV, visible and IR; in addition, gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered by the Earth's upper atmosphere before they can reach the surface, so it is this filtering, not an absence of these rays from the Sun, that protects life.
s: notes that only a small fraction of solar energy reaching Earth is gamma/X-ray, since ~99% is UV/visible/IR
explains that gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered by the Earth's upper atmosphere

questions.a: The claim is incorrect: the solar constant is measured at the top of the atmosphere before any absorption or scattering, while the actual insolation reaching the surface is lower (about 1 kWm-2 under clear sky) and varies with location and sky conditions.
s: disagrees with the claim

concepts.name: Albedo and Latitude: Why Heating Is Uneven
concepts.description: How a surface's albedo (its reflectivity) and a place's latitude both cause different parts of the Earth to heat unevenly, including the urban heat island effect.
concepts.idea: How much a surface warms depends on its albedo (how much sunlight it reflects versus absorbs) and on its latitude (how directly the Sun's rays strike it).
concepts.rule: High-albedo surfaces such as snow and ice reflect most incoming sunlight and stay cool; low-albedo surfaces such as black soil and ocean water absorb more and warm faster; separately, because Earth is a sphere, sunlight is concentrated over a smaller area at the equator and spread over a larger area near the poles, so equatorial regions stay warm and polar regions stay cold.
concepts.example: Snow has a very high albedo (0.80-0.90) and stays cold because it reflects most sunlight, while a dark, built-up city -- whose materials absorb and re-radiate heat -- becomes a noticeably warmer 'urban heat island' than the surrounding countryside.

concepts.name: The Atmosphere: Layers, Ozone and the Greenhouse Effect
concepts.description: The layered structure of the atmosphere, how the troposphere and stratosphere behave differently, and how the ozone layer and greenhouse gases together keep the Earth's surface at a life-supporting temperature.
concepts.idea: The atmosphere's layered structure and its greenhouse gases together determine both where weather happens and how warm the Earth stays.
concepts.rule: Almost all weather occurs in the troposphere (0-12 km), where temperature falls with height; in the stratosphere (12-50 km) the ozone layer absorbs UV and temperature rises with height, which calms the layer and confines weather below it; the atmosphere protects life by absorbing incoming UV (the ozone layer) and by trapping outgoing heat re-radiated from the surface (greenhouse gases like CO2, methane and water vapour) -- without this trapping, Earth would be too cold for life, but too much of it makes Earth too hot.
concepts.example: Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, because Venus's thick atmosphere causes an uncontrolled greenhouse effect that traps far more heat.

concepts.name: Winds and Ocean Currents
concepts.description: How uneven heating of the Earth's surface drives local winds (valley and mountain breezes), global planetary wind belts, and ocean currents, including gyres and the North Atlantic Drift.
concepts.idea: Wind and ocean currents are both driven by the same underlying cause -- uneven heating of the Earth by the Sun creating pressure and density differences -- just operating at different scales, from a single valley to the whole globe.
concepts.rule: Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure; locally this gives valley breezes (day) and mountain breezes (night); globally, heating differences between equator and poles create belts of low and high pressure that drive planetary winds, which the Earth's rotation deflects into curved paths; ocean currents are driven the same way -- by wind friction, temperature and salinity differences, and Earth's rotation -- forming clockwise gyres in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise gyres in the Southern Hemisphere.
concepts.example: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, carries warm equatorial water to north-western Europe and keeps many of its ports ice-free in winter even at high latitudes.

concepts.name: Biogeochemical Cycles: Water, Carbon, Nitrogen and Oxygen
concepts.description: How matter -- water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen -- cycles endlessly between living organisms and the non-living air, water, soil and rock around them, and how each named cycle actually works.
concepts.idea: Matter such as water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen is never used up -- it cycles endlessly between living organisms and the non-living air, water, soil and rock around them.
concepts.rule: In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses, precipitates and flows back to the ocean; in the carbon cycle, a fast biological loop (photosynthesis/respiration, days to years) and a slow geological loop (fossil fuel formation and burning, millions of years) both move carbon between atmosphere, biosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere; in the nitrogen cycle, bacteria must fix unreactive atmospheric N2 into usable compounds (fixation, nitrification, ammonification, denitrification) since plants and animals cannot use N2 directly; in the oxygen cycle, respiration and combustion consume O2 and release CO2, while photosynthesis restores it.
concepts.example: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium, living in the root nodules of legumes, convert unusable atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia that plants can actually absorb and use.

concepts.name: Human Impact on Earth's Processes
concepts.description: How human activities -- burning fossil fuels, overusing fertilisers and deforestation -- disrupt the biogeochemical balances described earlier in the chapter, and what local and global actions can help restore that balance.
concepts.idea: Human activity disrupts the same biogeochemical balances the chapter has just described -- adding excess carbon and nitrogen faster than natural cycles can absorb them, and changing land cover in ways that ripple across spheres -- but local action plus global cooperation can help restore that balance.
concepts.rule: Excess CO2 acidifies oceans and intensifies the greenhouse effect; excess fertiliser nitrogen causes eutrophication (algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish); deforestation reduces photosynthesis, transpiration and local rainfall, changes albedo, and increases soil erosion and biodiversity loss; global cooperation can work, as the Montreal Protocol shows for the ozone layer, while renewable energy, afforestation and sustainable practices help restore balance.
concepts.example: Overuse of fertilisers washes excess nitrate into rivers and lakes, triggering algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish -- a process called eutrophication.

questions.q: The process by which excess nutrients, such as nitrates, cause algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish is called ____.
questions.a: eutrophication

questions.q: The Montreal Protocol was a global agreement that successfully reduced the use of
questions.a: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)

questions.q: Excess CO2 absorbed by the oceans makes sea water more
questions.a: acidic

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as an effect of deforestation?
questions.a: increased ozone layer recovery

questions.q: Ground-level ozone and smog near cities are mainly formed when
questions.a: vehicular emissions react with sunlight
o: the stratospheric ozone layer descends to the ground

questions.q: India's initiative encouraging mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles, introduced at the UN Climate Change Conference in 2021, is called Mission ____.
questions.a: LiFE

questions.q: Why does warmer ocean water reduce the ocean's effectiveness as a carbon sink, according to the chapter?
questions.a: it reduces the ocean's capacity to absorb CO2
o: it reduces the ocean's capacity to absorb CO2
it causes the ocean to release oxygen instead of carbon dioxide

questions.q: Which of the following does the chapter describe as being LESS successful than the Montreal Protocol?
questions.a: the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement
o: the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement
the agreement that reduced CFC use
the agreement on ozone layer recovery

questions.q: Explain how deforestation can lead to both reduced local rainfall and increased soil erosion.
questions.a: Fewer trees means decreased photosynthesis and reduced transpiration, which can lead to a decline in local rainfall; without tree roots to hold the soil together, soil erosion increases.
s: states that decreased photosynthesis/transpiration from fewer trees can reduce local rainfall
states that without tree roots holding soil together, soil erosion increases

questions.q: A farmer notices thick algae covering a nearby pond after using large amounts of fertiliser on the surrounding fields. This is most likely an example of
questions.a: eutrophication

questions.q: Which individual action, mentioned in the chapter, could help restore the balance disturbed by human activity?
questions.a: saving water, food and energy, and reducing, reusing and recycling waste
o: saving water, food and energy, and reducing, reusing and recycling waste
burning more fossil fuels for convenience
clearing more forest land for farming
using more chemical fertiliser than needed

questions.q: Explain why the Montreal Protocol is considered a success story, according to the chapter, and what it shows about tackling global environmental problems.
questions.a: It reduced the use of CFCs, and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering; this shows the power of international scientific cooperation in solving environmental problems.
s: states that reducing CFCs has let the ozone layer slowly recover
states that this shows the power of global/international cooperation

questions.q: A lake near farmland develops an algal bloom every year after the fertilising season. Explain the chain of events leading from fertiliser use to fish dying in the lake.
questions.a: Excess nitrogen (nitrate) from the fertiliser runs off into the lake; this causes widespread growth of algae, an algal bloom, which depletes the lake's oxygen and then kills the fish -- this whole process is called eutrophication.
s: states that excess nitrogen/nitrate from fertiliser runs off into the lake
states that this causes an algal bloom that depletes oxygen and kills fish

questions.q: Why does the chapter describe deforestation as having effects 'across air, water, land and living organisms' rather than just one effect?
questions.a: because clearing forests changes rainfall, albedo, soil erosion and biodiversity all at once, touching every sphere
o: because clearing forests changes rainfall, albedo, soil erosion and biodiversity all at once, touching every sphere
because deforestation only ever affects the atmosphere
because deforestation has no measurable effects at all
because deforestation only affects a single species of tree

questions.q: Choose one human activity described in the chapter (such as burning fossil fuels, overusing fertilisers, or deforestation) and trace its effects through at least three different Earth spheres, explaining the chain of cause and effect at each step.
questions.a: For example, deforestation directly affects the biosphere by destroying habitats and reducing plant cover; this reduces photosynthesis and transpiration, altering the atmosphere by lowering local rainfall and changing the surface albedo; without tree roots to hold it, soil is also washed away more easily, affecting the geosphere through increased erosion.
s: names one human activity from the chapter
correctly describes its first direct effect on one sphere
correctly traces the effect through at least one more connected sphere, showing a chain of cause and effect

questions.q: Consider: (I) Ground-level ozone formed from vehicular emissions is harmful to health. (II) The ozone layer in the stratosphere is also harmful to health in the same way. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Compare the Montreal Protocol with the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, based on what the chapter says about their outcomes.
questions.a: The Montreal Protocol succeeded in reducing CFCs and helping the ozone layer recover; the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, both aimed at reducing CO2 emissions, have been less successful, according to the chapter.
s: correctly states the Montreal Protocol succeeded in reducing CFCs, helping ozone recovery
correctly states the Kyoto Protocol/Paris Agreement have been less successful

questions.q: The chapter contrasts the success of the Montreal Protocol with the more limited success of the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement. Suggest one possible reason the ozone problem was easier to solve globally than the CO2/climate problem, using ideas from the chapter about how central fossil fuels and CO2 are to human activity.
questions.a: The Montreal Protocol succeeded in reducing CFCs, letting the ozone layer recover, while the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, aimed at reducing CO2 emissions, have been less successful. A likely reason is that CFCs were used in a narrower range of products, such as refrigerators and aerosols, and could be replaced without disrupting most of the economy, whereas fossil fuels and the CO2 they release are central to energy, transport, industry and daily life almost everywhere, making global cooperation to cut them much harder to achieve.
s: correctly states the outcome contrast: Montreal Protocol succeeded; Kyoto/Paris less successful
gives a plausible reason connected to the chapter, e.g. CFCs were narrower in use while fossil fuels/CO2 are far more central to daily life and industry
draws a reasoned conclusion linking this difference to why global cooperation is harder for CO2 than for CFCs

questions.q: A classmate argues that since India is 'rapidly increasing renewable energy,' fossil fuels no longer matter for India's emissions. Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect: the chapter states that fossil fuels still generate a significant part of India's electricity and contribute harmful emissions, even though the rapid growth of renewable energy, especially solar, offers hope for the future.
s: disagrees with the claim
justifies using the chapter's statement that fossil fuels still generate significant electricity and emissions in India even as renewables grow

questions.q: Design three practical actions (different from those directly listed in the chapter, but in the same spirit) that a school could take to help restore the balance disturbed by human activity, and explain how each connects to an idea from the chapter (such as the carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, deforestation or the greenhouse effect).
questions.a: For example: (1) The school could set up a compost pit for food waste instead of sending it to landfill, returning nutrients to the soil rather than releasing methane, connecting to the carbon cycle. (2) The school could plant a small vegetable garden using minimal fertiliser and natural pest control, connecting to the nitrogen cycle and avoiding eutrophication of nearby water bodies. (3) The school could install solar panels on its roof to reduce its use of fossil-fuel electricity, connecting to the greenhouse effect and reducing its CO2 emissions.
s: proposes three distinct, practical actions
each action is genuinely different from ones directly named in the chapter
each action is correctly connected to a relevant idea from the chapter
